The temperature-dependent engineering elastic constants of a DS nickel-base superalloy were estimated from the single-crystal elastic constants of nickel and MAR-MOO2 superalloy.
The DS superalloy was modeled as a transversely isotropic material with five independent elastic constants.
The five independent elastic constants of the DS material (A, C, F, L, and N) were expressed in terms of the three independent elastic constants of the cubic single crystal.
The temperature-dependent stiffness coefficients (C11, C12, and C44) for single-crystal nickel were obtained by fitting second-degree polynomials to the data from the literature.
The compliance coefficients (S11, S12, and S44) for single-crystal nickel were calculated from the stiffness coefficients.
The temperature-dependent engineering elastic constants for the DS nickel-base superalloy, including Young's moduli, shear moduli, and Poisson's ratios, were tabulated and plotted.
The temperature-dependent compliance coefficients for single-crystal MAR-MOO2 were obtained from the literature, and the engineering elastic constants for DS MAR-MOO2 were calculated.
The estimated longitudinal elastic modulus of DS MAR-M246 from the SC MAR-MOO2 data was closer to the experimental values than the estimation from SC nickel data.
The Wells method assumes a transversely isotropic material, which may not be valid for DS superalloys with a small number of grains in the transverse direction.

No experimentally determined temperature-dependent transverse modulus, shear moduli, and Poisson's ratios were available for DS nickel-base superalloys to verify the accuracy of the estimated engineering elastic constants.
The engineering elastic constants determined in this study are applicable only when a large number of grains are present along the transverse direction in a DS nickel-base superalloy.
The results of this study can be used as input for performing finite element structural analysis of directionally solidified turbine engine components.
The Wells method can be used to estimate the engineering elastic constants of any directionally solidified material from the elastic constants of the corresponding cubic single crystal.
The primary orientation of both the single crystal and the DS superalloy was assumed to be along the [001] direction.
The DS superalloy was assumed to have a sufficiently large number of columnar grains to be modeled as a transversely isotropic material.
